figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Tokenization with States (TWS). Each session records a different set of neurons. TWS segments every trial into behavioral states at task events and converts each state into tokens without neuron identity, so all sessions share one token space. States S0 to S2 are the states k=1, 2, 3 of Algorithm 1, and τ1 and τ2 are the event times shifted by two trainable offsets shared by all sessions.

Table 1: Cross-session decoding on IBL over the 53 held-out sessions (Section 4.1). ±: SD over 5 model seeds. PCA and Population Statistics have no trained model; CEBRA and NEDS train one model per session and are run once.

Table 2: Tokenization boundary ablation (IBL, 53 held-out sessions). Every row uses the same architecture and only the boundaries change. (a) Number of boundaries. (b) Boundary placement at fixed K=3. Jittered: true boundary plus Gaussian noise with standard deviation σ bins. Fixed: boundary at a constant bin for all trials. Random: uniform draw per trial. Shuffled: real boundaries reassigned across (or within) sessions. Jitter and shuffling move only the boundaries that exist: a trial whose first movement falls outside the window keeps none, as in the true condition. Eventtime information: the same probe on the one-hot first-movement bin that each condition gives, with no neural data; it measures how much of the label that input holds (mean over 5 draws of the perturbation). Cross-session leave-one-session-out, as in Table 1. ±: SD over 5 model seeds, each with its own boundary randomization.
Table 3: Tokenizer × backbone on IBL (53 held-out sessions, cross-session protocol of Table 1); every model learns from scratch. ±: SD over 5 model seeds. The CNN row repeats Table 1.

Table 4: Transfer of the frozen representation with a linear probe; POYO trains on each dataset (protocol in Section 4.1). MCC, mean ± SD over 5 seeds. Rows without ± are deterministic features. Event-time information uses the first-movement bin and no neural data.

Figure 2: Training organizes the TWS embedding space around behavior; the tokenizer decides how far. (A) Each IBL session contributes two points, the mean embedding of its trials with (blue) and without (gray) a first movement within 2 s, and a line joins the two; PCA of these 486 points (first seed). Separation: distance between the two behavior centres over the spread of sessions around them, mean ± SD over 5 seeds. (B) Share of trial-embedding variance explained by session identity and, after removing each session’s mean, by movement (mean over seeds). Models trained without the 53 held-out sessions; embeddings of all 243 sessions.

Figure 3: Session invariance and data efficiency. (A) Session identifiability (normalized MI of a 243-class probe, x-axis) versus cross-session movement MCC (y-axis, the values of Table 1); methods in the upper-left corner achieve invariance without sacrificing decoding. We draw no error bars because the SD over 5 model seeds is smaller than the markers (values in Appendix Y). (B) Reaction time R2 versus number of decoder-training sessions (log scale). Shaded bands: ±1 SD over 5 model seeds for TWS and over 20 draws of decoder-training sessions for the baselines. Session identifiability over all 243 IBL sessions; TWS and PerceiverIO decoding over the 53 heldout sessions, with decoder-training sessions in (B) drawn from the other 190.
Table 5: How much of each target survives a change of the recorded neurons. MCC, averaged over sessions.
Table 6: Training hyperparameters. The six IBL behavioral heads are choice, feedback, licking, movement, wheel velocity and RT. New-dataset training follows Appendix N.

Table 10: Behavioral variable definitions. Type A: encoded across the population, recoverable from any sufficiently large neuronal subset. Type B: depends on which specific neurons are recorded. Scale: C = classification, R = regression. ∗Feedback is structurally Type A but its cross-session decodability is dominated by its correlation with movement.
Table 11: Class distributions and base rates for the 7 IBL behavioral variables (243 sessions, 152,794 trials). P (positive): proportion of positive class. σcross(µ): std of per-session means.

Table 12: Full results on all 7 IBL behavioral variables. MCC for classification; R2 for wheel velocity and RT, with RT standardized per session across sessions and raw within sessions. Crosssession: leave-one-session-out Ridge probe, scored on the 53 held-out sessions. Within-session: TWS and PerceiverIO are probed on the trials of the 53 held-out sessions pooled (random 60/20/20 split, 5 repeats), which none of them trained on; POYO and Population Statistics on the trials of all sessions pooled; PCA, firing rates and CEBRA, whose feature spaces differ between sessions, per session (random 60/20/20 split). ±: SD over 5 model seeds; rows without ± are a single run. PerceiverIO uses the same CNN backbone as TWS. Aligned and unaligned PCA are scored on four variables only (Appendix D). Per-variable class distributions in Appendix L.
Table 14: Whisker motion energy and pupil diameter (R2) on the 5 held-out IBL sessions with video. Mean ± SD over 5 model seeds.

Figure 4: TWS states occupy orthogonal subspaces with distinct dimensionality. (A) Sessiondemeaned PCA of state centroids (243 sessions; pretrained model, first seed). Small dots: persession centroids; large circles: grand means; gray lines connect the three states within individual sessions. (B) Cumulative explained variance per state. Diamonds mark each state’s participation ratio (PR, effective dimensionality). Colors and state labels match Figure 1.

Table 15: Regime boundary timing decomposition (226 IBL sessions, within-session 5-fold CV Ridge on raw state means x̄k ∈ R3N , mean ± std across sessions). Not directly comparable to cross-session R2 in Table 1.
Figure 5: Session means of every tokenizer × backbone × training combination, drawn as in Figure 2A.
Figure 6: What the trial-embedding variance of each combination is made of, drawn as in Figure 2B.
Figure 7: Linear CKA between the trial embeddings of every combination (first seed, 20,000 shared trials).
Table 22: How each target is defined and what the boundary position alone decodes (MCC; RT: R2).

Figure 8: State tokens of TWS pretrained (the 53 held-out sessions excluded from training) for all 243 IBL sessions. (A) t-SNE of 2,400 state tokens (800 per state) colored by state. (B) The same coordinates colored by recording lab. (C) Silhouette scores of the t-SNE coordinates for state, lab, subject and session.

Figure 9: 2D t-SNE of the trial embeddings of 10 held-out IBL sessions. Top: one color per session. Bottom: the same maps of TWS pretrained + finetuned, TWS (random init) and CEBRA, colored by whether the mouse moved within 2 s. POYO and PCA separate the sessions, while TWS mixes them and still separates the two behaviors. Nearby trials from other sessions share the movement label above chance for TWS pretrained + finetuned (+0.13), but hardly for TWS (random init) (+0.03) or CEBRA (+0.02), whose separate per-session models overlap only by chance (15 nearest neighbors from other sessions).
Figure 10: Session identifiability (normalized MI of a 39-class probe) against cross-session movement accuracy on the 39 Steinmetz sessions. Mean ± SD over 5 model seeds.
Table 31: Direction consistency, five-session decoding and session identification on the 53 held-out IBL sessions (mean over 5 model seeds). PerceiverIO uses the same CNN backbone as TWS.
